title: Geometry-Aware Preference Optimization for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

paper.title: Geometry-Aware Preference Optimization for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Preference alignment has become a standard practice for text-to-image diffusion models. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) simplifies this process by eliminating explicit reward modeling. Its diffusion variant, Diffusion-DPO, has become a widely adopted baseline. Diffusion-DPO essentially encourages the likelihood of preferred samples while suppressing dispreferred ones. In this paper, we revisit DPO-style alignment methods for diffusion models from the perspective of the manifold hypothesis. Under this view, natural images concentrate near a low-dimensional manifold embedded in the high-dimensional ambient space, whereas DPO directly optimizes preference distributions in the full space without accounting for this geometric structure. This creates a mismatch in the optimization dynamics: it suppresses geometry-preserving tangential updates, while insufficiently restricting hazardous normal-direction updates. This mismatch gradually degrades image quality and diversity. To address this issue, we propose A nisotropic Geometry-Aware P reference O ptimization ( APO ), which replaces the uniform Euclidean treatment of prediction errors with a geometry-aware anisotropic metric derived from the reference model. Concretely, APO adaptively strengthens regularization in directions where the reference denoising function is highly sensitive, while relaxing constraints in directions that permit safe semantic adjustment. This recalibrates preference optimization according to the local manifold geometry, and maintains the original manifold structure. Experiments show that APO achieves strong performance and an average win rate exceeding 60% against various existing alignment methods across diverse benchmarks. It requires significantly fewer training steps than prior methods, and preserves generation diversity throughout training.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have achieved remarkable progress in recent years, enabling high-fidelity and semantically controllable image synthesis across diverse domains [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Inspired by the success of reinforcement learning for alignment in large language models, a growing number of post-training strategies have recently been introduced for diffusion models to improve human preference alignment, aesthetic quality, and prompt consistency [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Most existing approaches rely on training a reward model to learn preference signals and guide policy optimization. Diffusion-DPO [ 10 ] , which adapts Direct Preference Optimization [ 11 ] to diffusion models, has emerged as a practical alignment approach. It directly optimizes pairwise preferences through implicit likelihood comparisons while avoiding explicit reward model training, substantially simplifying the alignment pipeline. Following Diffusion-DPO, numerous variants have been proposed to improve aspects such as reward modeling, sampling efficiency, optimization stability, and model adaptability in diffusion alignment [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] . Despite these advances, we find that DPO-based alignment of diffusion models still suffers from a previously overlooked geometric failure mode: off-manifold drift. The manifold hypothesis posits that natural image distributions concentrate near a low-dimensional manifold embedded in the ambient latent denoising space [ 16 , 17 ] . In diffusion models, preference optimization is performed in the noisy latent denoising space conditioned on the text prompt, where the local geometry evolves across diffusion timesteps. However, although preference signals are ultimately defined over natural images, optimization is still performed in the full high-dimensional latent denoising space without considering the intrinsic geometry of the underlying data manifold. In particular, existing DPO-style objectives [ 10 ] optimize denoising prediction errors under an isotropic Euclidean metric, implicitly treating all perturbation directions in the latent space equally. This leads to two consequences: • Updates along manifold-normal directions can easily push samples away from the natural image manifold, causing semantic distortion and quality degradation. Without explicit suppression of these geometry-sensitive directions, off-manifold drift accumulates during alignment. • Updates along manifold-tangent directions are generally safer and often capture semantically meaningful variations. However, they are constrained by the same uniform regularization strength, unnecessarily limiting flexible semantic adjustments in preference optimization. While some prior works have incorporated manifold-aware geometric constraints into generative dynamics, such considerations remain largely unexplored in post-training preference alignment for pretrained diffusion models. To address this issue, we propose Anisotropic Geometry-Aware Preference Optimization (APO) . APO constructs a Jacobian-induced anisotropic metric from the local score-field geometry of the frozen reference model, adaptively suppressing updates along geometry-sensitive normal directions while allowing more flexible exploration along manifold-aligned tangent directions. To make the method computationally practical, we further derive an efficient forward-only approximation based on Hutchinson estimation and finite differences, eliminating the expensive reference-model backward pass while preserving the geometric regularization effect. Our key observations and technical contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify off-manifold drift as a fundamental geometric failure mode in DPO-based diffusion alignment, and provide theoretical and empirical analyses connecting this phenomenon to isotropic optimization in high-dimensional denoising space. • We propose APO, a Jacobian-induced anisotropic preference optimization framework together with an efficient forward-only Hutchinson finite-difference approximation, enabling scalable geometry-aware diffusion alignment without reference-model backpropagation. • Extensive experiments on SD1.5 and SDXL across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that APO consistently improves alignment quality, image realism, semantic preservation, and generation diversity while maintaining strong training efficiency.

sections.heading: Diffusion Models for Visual Generation
sections.text: Diffusion models have emerged as the dominant paradigm for image synthesis due to their training stability and high sample quality [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] . The introduction of latent diffusion substantially reduced computational costs by operating the denoising process in a compressed representation space, enabling high-resolution text-to-image generation at scale [ 1 ] . This architecture catalyzed a series of large-scale open-weight models, including SDXL [ 2 ] , SD3 [ 3 ] , and the FLUX series [ 4 ] , which form the backbone of most contemporary visual generation research. However, diffusion models are often trained on large-scale general-purpose datasets with varying quality, which tends to introduce biases that deviate from human preferences. Therefore, aligning diffusion models with human preferences is a highly necessary practice.

sections.heading: Reward-Based Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion
sections.text: Early post-training efforts adopt supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on curated high-quality image-text pairs [ 22 ] . While effective, SFT inherently treats all samples equally and does not capture the comparative nature of human preference. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) [ 23 , 24 ] addresses this by first training a proxy reward model on human annotations and then optimizing the diffusion policy with policy gradient methods such as DDPO [ 5 ] and DPOK [ 6 ] , or by directly backpropagating differentiable rewards as in DRaFT [ 8 ] and AlignProp [ 7 ] . These approaches, however, are prone to reward overoptimization. To bypass explicit reward learning, Diffusion-DPO [ 10 ] adapts Direct Preference Optimization to diffusion models, enabling offline fine-tuning directly on pairwise preference data without a separate reward model. Subsequently, a series of methods have been proposed to address the weaknesses of Diffusion-DPO in various aspects, including sampling efficiency, reward estimation, model adaptability, and reward diversity [ 25 , 12 , 26 , 13 , 27 , 15 , 28 , 29 ] . In addition, online reinforcement learning methods such as Flow-GRPO [ 9 ] and DanceGRPO [ 30 ] have become an increasingly popular paradigm. Some of these approaches seek to unify tasks spanning text-to-image, text-to-video, and image-to-video generation within a single framework, while others focus on improving computational efficiency [ 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 ] . While existing alignment methods primarily modify the reward formulation, optimization strategy, or sampling efficiency, our work instead revisits the geometric assumptions underlying the optimization metric itself.

sections.heading: Manifold Learning for Diffusion
sections.text: The manifold hypothesis posits that high-dimensional natural data concentrate near a low-dimensional submanifold of the ambient space [ 16 , 17 ] . In the context of diffusion models, this connection is theoretically well-grounded: the score function is intimately related to the geometry of the data distribution and approximates the normal bundle of the data manifold [ 20 , 36 , 37 , 38 ] , a structural prior that has motivated a rich line of research connecting manifold learning with generative modeling [ 39 , 40 , 41 , 38 , 42 ] . Furthermore, manifold awareness has proven essential for improving inference-time quality, as demonstrated by CFG++ [ 43 ] , TCFG [ 44 ] , and Be Tangential to Manifold [ 45 ] . However, in the domain of preference alignment for diffusion models based on standard Euclidean diffusion parameterizations, manifold learning theory has yet to be considered.

sections.heading: 3 Background and Motivation
sections.text: In this section, we first review diffusion models and the formulation of Diffusion-DPO. We then revisit the DPO objective from a geometric perspective and show that its isotropic optimization mechanism can induce harmful off-manifold drift during preference alignment.

sections.heading: 3.3 Off-Manifold Drift in Diffusion-DPO
sections.text: As discussed in Section 3.2 , the training objective in Diffusion-DPO compares the prediction errors of the winner and the loser samples using a uniform Euclidean metric, treating all reverse-trajectory update directions in ℝ D \mathbb{R}^{D} equally. Under the manifold hypothesis [ 16 , 17 ] , however, natural data concentrate near a low-dimensional latent submanifold ℳ ⊂ ℝ D \mathcal{M}\subset\mathbb{R}^{D} , and the ambient space locally decomposes into tangent directions T x ​ ℳ T_{x}\mathcal{M} and normal directions N x ​ ℳ N_{x}\mathcal{M} . These directions play fundamentally different geometric roles. Reverse-trajectory displacements along tangent directions tend to preserve semantic consistency and remain close to the data manifold, whereas displacements along normal directions are more likely to move trajectories away from the manifold and degrade image quality. DPO-style diffusion alignment methods measure all trajectory-update discrepancies isotropically under the same Euclidean geometry, without distinguishing geometry-preserving directions from geometry-sensitive ones. As a result, updates along geometry-sensitive manifold-normal directions are insufficiently constrained, while manifold-aligned tangent directions become unnecessarily restricted for semantic adjustment. We refer to this geometric failure mode as off-manifold drift . We illustrate this phenomenon with a minimal example ( Figure 1 ), where a DDPM pretrained on a unit circle embedded in ℝ 32 \mathbb{R}^{32} is fine-tuned. In this setup, the left semicircle corresponds to low-reward (loser) regions, while the right semicircle corresponds to high-reward (winner) regions. For each preference pair, we randomly sample one point from each semicircle and designate the point from the right semicircle as the winner. We compare DPO and its Euclidean-metric variants, all of which progressively shift probability mass toward the preferred region, yet exhibit noticeable off-manifold drift during training, producing large numbers of off-manifold samples ( red ). This observation motivates the central question of our work: can we design a geometry-aware anisotropic regularizer that adapts to the local structure of the diffusion representation space? We provide a positive answer in the next section.

sections.heading: 4 Method
sections.text: To address this issue, we introduce Anisotropic Geometry-Aware Preference Optimization (APO), which replaces the isotropic Euclidean penalty in Diffusion-DPO with a Jacobian-induced anisotropic geometry. Our method consists of three components: • In subsection 4.1 , we derive a local geometric characterization of the diffusion model via the Jacobian of the reference score field, which reveals an anisotropic decomposition into tangential and normal directions on the data manifold. • In subsection 4.2 , we construct a Jacobian-induced quadratic form that defines a Riemannian metric on the noise prediction space, leading to an anisotropic preference optimization objective. • In subsection 4.3 , we provide an efficient implementation for integrating our method into the diffusion alignment framework to streamline the computation. sections.text: Under the manifold hypothesis, natural data concentrate near a low-dimensional latent submanifold ℳ ⊂ ℝ D \mathcal{M}\subset\mathbb{R}^{D} . In particular, prior work has shown that its local variation exhibits anisotropy aligned with the underlying manifold structure [ 20 , 36 , 37 , 16 ] : directions corresponding to rapid density change are associated with off-manifold (normal) perturbations, while directions with slow variation correspond to on-manifold (tangent) perturbations. sections.heading: Single-probe stability
sections.text: Although the Hutchinson estimator in Equation 19 is a stochastic approximation, a single probe direction ( n v = 1 n_{v}=1 ) is already sufficient in practice. The resulting optimization remains highly stable, and this behavior arises from the temporal coherence of diffusion trajectories themselves. APO does not require recovering the full Jacobian structure at each timestep. The objective only depends on the dominant anisotropic direction induced by J ref ⊤ ​ δ t J_{\mathrm{ref}}^{\top}\delta_{t} . Along the diffusion trajectory, nearby timesteps share highly correlated geometric structure and similar local manifold orientation. As a result, although a single probe may introduce instantaneous stochasticity, its projected direction repeatedly aligns with the same underlying anisotropic component across neighboring noise scales. Consequently, the stochastic errors introduced by individual probes tend to fluctuate inconsistently across timesteps, while the persistent geometric component accumulates coherently throughout optimization. This creates a natural temporal averaging effect along the diffusion trajectory: unstable probe noise is progressively canceled, whereas stable manifold-aware directions are repeatedly reinforced. In practice, this reduces the variance to a low level, making n v = 1 n_{v}=1 already sufficient to produce stable optimization dynamics. Naturally, increasing the number of probe directions can further improve the accuracy and stability of the anisotropic estimate. However, the empirical gains quickly exhibit diminishing returns relative to the additional computational cost. Therefore, we retain the multi-probe formulation in Algorithm 1 for completeness, and provide a detailed ablation study on n v n_{v} in Section 5.3.3 .

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: Our experiments seek to answer three questions: • Does APO improve preference alignment quality and generation behavior across architectures and benchmarks? • Are the gains truly attributable to the proposed Jacobian-induced anisotropic geometry? • Under what regimes is the geometric regularization most beneficial? subsection 5.2 presents the main quantitative and qualitative results. subsection 5.3 provides ablations and detailed analyses of the underlying geometric mechanism.

sections.heading: Models, Datasets, and Baselines
sections.text: We conduct experiments on two widely used text-to-image backbones, Stable Diffusion 1.5 (SD1.5) and Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL) [ 2 ] . All models are fine-tuned on the Pick-a-Pic v2 dataset [ 46 ] , which provides 851,293 training preference pairs over 58,960 distinct prompts after removing ties. We compare our method against the unmodified base models (SD1.5 and SDXL), supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on winner images [ 22 ] , Diffusion-DPO [ 10 ] , InPO [ 13 ] , and Diffusion-SDPO [ 14 ] . Additionally, on SD1.5, we also compare against Diffusion-KTO [ 12 ] , and on SDXL, we additionally compare against LPO [ 15 ] . All the above baselines employ the uniform Euclidean treatment of prediction errors. Our experiments are evaluated on the HPSv2 [ 47 ] , Parti-Prompts [ 48 ] and Pick-a-Picv2 [ 46 ] test sets, following standard protocols.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: We assess alignment quality using three reward models that capture human preference: PickScore [ 46 ] , HPS [ 47 ] , and the LAION Aesthetic Predictor [ 49 ] . We further report CLIP score [ 50 ] for text-image alignment. Furthermore, we conducted a human evaluation on SDXL across four dimensions. We recruited 40 professional participants, each evaluating 50 different sets of images. Each set included the base model, DPO, and APO, with the order randomly shuffled. For each set, participants rated images across four dimensions: text-content alignment, image realism, aesthetic quality, and overall preference. We also evaluated the training efficiency on HPSv2 for SD1.5 and SDXL: we report the single-GPU (NVIDIA A100) training hours and peak GPU memory (GB) on SD1.5 and SDXL, along with a comparison against the standard DPO method.

sections.heading: Qualitative Results
sections.text: Figure 5 and Figure 10 presents representative generations from SD1.5 and SDXL under different preference optimization methods. APO consistently produces images with higher visual fidelity, more natural object structures, and better fine-grained details than standard Diffusion-DPO and related baselines. The generated samples also exhibit more coherent global composition. These observations are consistent with our geometric interpretation: by suppressing unstable updates in sensitive directions, APO better preserves the underlying structure learned by the reference diffusion model during alignment.

sections.heading: Training Efficiency
sections.text: We report the training efficiency of DPO and APO on SD1.5 and SDXL, including Total Training Hours (h) and peak GPU memory (GB). As shown in Table 2 , APO reduces total training time to roughly half of standard Diffusion-DPO on both models. This speedup mainly comes from faster convergence and fewer training steps. APO reaches stable performance within approximately 900 training steps, whereas standard Diffusion-DPO typically requires around 2000 steps under the same training setup . This faster convergence is empirically supported by the training dynamics shown in Figure 6 , where APO’s scores ascend sharply within the first 1,000 steps and stabilize smoothly, while DPO still exhibits a gradual climb and requires nearly twice the steps to reach a comparable plateau. Although APO introduces an additional forward evaluation for Jacobian estimation, it stabilizes the alignment process by anchoring optimization in more reliable geometric directions. As a result, APO requires significantly fewer training steps, and benefits from weaker KL regularization without sacrificing stability. In terms of memory, APO only increases peak GPU usage by around 5% compared with DPO. The additional forward pass introduces negligible memory overhead, since no extra backpropagation graph is stored.

sections.heading: Distributional Stability During Alignment
sections.text: To further examine the effect of preference optimization on the overall generation distribution, we track the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) throughout training on the COCO-2017 benchmark using the standard FID-50K protocol. Lower FID indicates closer agreement between the generated and reference image distributions. As shown in Figure 7 , standard preference optimization methods exhibit a clear tendency toward increasing FID as training progresses. On SD1.5, the FID of DPO, KTO, SDPO, and InPO generally increases throughout training, with DPO showing the largest degradation. In contrast, APO steadily reduces FID from around 20 to approximately 16.65 . A similar trend is observed on SDXL, where DPO, SDPO, InPO, and LPO all exhibit an overall increase in FID, while APO remains at a substantially lower level throughout training and reaches approximately 16.23 at the end of alignment.

sections.heading: 5.3.1 Study on Reward Metrics and Image Quality.
sections.text: We evaluate APO against three critical baselines on the HPSv2 benchmark: (a) standard DPO; (b) Our APO; (c) a time-threshold variant where APO is applied only on timesteps t ≥ t τ t\geq t_{\tau} and standard DPO is used for t < t τ t<t_{\tau} . We vary t τ ∈ { 200,400,600,800 } t_{\tau}\in\{200,400,600,800\} and report performance on the HPSv2 benchmark. As shown in Figure 8 , the time-threshold results reveal a clear trend: performance decreases monotonically as t τ t_{\tau} increases (i.e., as APO is restricted to higher noise levels). The most significant drop occurs between t τ = 400 t_{\tau}=400 and t τ = 600 t_{\tau}=600 , suggesting that the intermediate noise range (approximately 400–600 steps) is where the anisotropic regularization provides the greatest benefit. The decline from t τ = 200 t_{\tau}=200 to t τ = 400 t_{\tau}=400 is moderate, while the gaps from t τ = 600 t_{\tau}=600 to 800 800 and from t τ = 800 t_{\tau}=800 to full DPO are notably smaller. These observations are consistent with the theoretical analysis in Section 4.4 . At low noise levels (small t t , near the clean image), the data manifold is well-defined and the Jacobian is maximally anisotropic; however, the generation process at this stage mainly refines fine-grained details (textures, fur, edges), which have limited impact on global preference scores. Hence, replacing APO with DPO in the low-noise region (i.e., setting t τ = 200 t_{\tau}=200 ) causes only a modest degradation. In contrast, the intermediate noise range (roughly 400–600 steps) is commonly associated with the formation of semantic layout and coarse structures—where off-manifold drift appears to have the strongest impact on alignment quality. The sharp performance drop when APO is omitted from this region highlights its critical role. At high noise levels (large t t ), the Jacobian becomes nearly isotropic, and APO naturally degenerates to DPO; therefore, restricting APO to very high timesteps ( t τ = 800 t_{\tau}=800 ) yields diminishing performance gains. Nevertheless, we still recommend applying APO across all timesteps, because even the high-noise region offers a slight but consistent advantage over full DPO.

sections.heading: 5.3.2 Diversity Preservation During Alignment.
sections.text: We investigate whether APO preserves generation diversity during preference optimization using perceptual and semantic diversity metrics tracked throughout training. fig. 9(a) (left) reports LPIPS Mean Pairwise Distance (MPD) [ 51 ] , which measures perceptual diversity among samples generated from the same prompt. APO consistently maintains higher diversity than standard DPO across both metrics throughout training, and the gap further widens as training progresses. Standard DPO applies uniform optimization pressure in all directions, causing the distribution to progressively contract toward narrow reward-seeking modes. In contrast, APO preserves greater flexibility along manifold tangent directions while suppressing unstable updates along geometry-sensitive directions. This anisotropic constraint helps maintain greater variation during alignment. (a) LPIPS Mean Pairwise Distance (MPD). (b) DINO feature variance. sections.heading: 5.3.3 Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis
sections.text: Table 3 reports the sensitivity of APO to its key hyperparameters: geometry strength λ \lambda , DPO regularization coefficient β \beta , finite-difference perturbation radius r r , and number of probe directions n v n_{v} .

sections.heading: Anisotropic regularization coefficient λ \lambda
sections.text: Setting λ = 0 \lambda=0 recovers standard Diffusion-DPO and yields the lowest scores across all metrics, confirming that the anisotropic correction is essential rather than merely additive regularization. Once the geometric term is added ( λ > 0 \lambda>0 ), performance improves immediately. We adopt λ = 0.8 \lambda=0.8 as the default.

sections.heading: DPO temperature β \beta
sections.text: We observe that APO achieves its best performance with a smaller β \beta than standard Diffusion-DPO and related implicit-reward alignment methods. Empirically, introducing the anisotropic geometric term already reshapes the optimization landscape by reweighting prediction discrepancies according to the local geometry induced by the reference Jacobian. As a result, strong global preference scaling becomes less necessary for achieving effective alignment. This observation is also consistent with the improved training efficiency reported in section 5.2 , where APO converges with substantially fewer optimization steps and faster alignment dynamics than standard Diffusion-DPO.

sections.heading: Perturbation radius r r
sections.text: APO is not sensitive to the numerical value of the perturbation radius; comparable performance is achieved for r r between 10 − 4 10^{-4} and 10 − 2 10^{-2} , with an optimum at r = 10 − 3 r=10^{-3} . Larger values ( r = 10 − 1 r=10^{-1} ) cause the finite-difference approximation to exit the linear regime of ϵ ref \epsilon_{\text{ref}} , introducing bias. Smaller values ( r = 10 − 4 r=10^{-4} ) show degraded performance, possibly due to numerical instability.

sections.heading: Number of probe directions n v n_{v}
sections.text: A single probe direction ( n v = 1 n_{v}=1 ) already achieves strong results, and increasing n v n_{v} yields only marginal gains. This is consistent with the analysis in Section 4.4 : the diffusion trajectory itself already induces strong temporal averaging of the anisotropic direction estimates, making single-probe estimation sufficiently stable in practice.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we presented APO, a geometry-aware preference optimization framework for diffusion models. We revisit diffusion preference alignment from the perspective of manifold geometry, and identify off-manifold drift as a fundamental failure mode induced by isotropic optimization in high-dimensional denoising space. To address this issue, APO constructs a Jacobian-induced anisotropic metric from the reference score field, selectively suppressing geometry-sensitive directions while preserving flexible exploration along manifold-aligned directions. Our results suggest that incorporating intrinsic geometric structure into preference optimization provides an effective and principled direction for robust diffusion alignment.

sections.heading: Limitation
sections.text: APO assumes that the reference score field provides a meaningful local approximation of the underlying data manifold. When the preference data distribution itself contains substantial off-manifold corruption or systematically noisy annotations, the induced geometry may become less reliable and potentially bias the alignment process. This may limit the effectiveness of APO in heavily distribution-shifted or weakly curated preference-learning scenarios. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.04980v1 [cs.CV] 04 Oct 2026 Geometry-Aware Preference Optimization for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models Journal: Pattern Recognition Lei Wang Email: likwang259@gmail.com Corresponding author: Corresponding author Affiliation: Sun Yat-Sen University, Guangzhou, China Zhen Wang Affiliation: Sun Yat-Sen University, Guangzhou, China Yuexiang Xie Affiliation: Alibaba Group, Hangzhou, China Yaliang Li Affiliation: Alibaba Group, Hangzhou, China Abstract Preference alignment has become a standard practice for text-to-image diffusion models. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) simplifies this process by eliminating explicit reward modeling. Its diffusion variant, Diffusion-DPO, has become a widely adopted baseline. Diffusion-DPO essentially encourages the likelihood of preferred samples while suppressing dispreferred ones. In this paper, we revisit DPO-style alignment methods for diffusion models from the perspective of the manifold hypothesis. Under this view, natural images concentrate near a low-dimensional manifold embedded in the high-dimensional ambient space, whereas DPO directly optimizes preference distributions in the full space without accounting for this geometric structure. This creates a mismatch in the optimization dynamics: it suppresses geometry-preserving tangential updates, while insufficiently restricting hazardous normal-direction updates. This mismatch gradually degrades image quality and diversity. To address this issue, we propose A nisotropic Geometry-Aware P reference O ptimization ( APO ), which replaces the uniform Euclidean treatment of prediction errors with a geometry-aware anisotropic metric derived from the reference model. Concretely, APO adaptively strengthens regularization in directions where the reference denoising function is highly sensitive, while relaxing constraints in directions that permit safe semantic adjustment. This recalibrates preference optimization according to the local manifold geometry, and maintains the original manifold structure. Experiments show that APO achieves strong performance and an average win rate exceeding 60% against various existing alignment methods across diverse benchmarks. It requires significantly fewer training steps than prior methods, and preserves generation diversity throughout training. Keywords: Diffusion Models , Text-to-Image Generation , Direct Preference Optimization 1 Introduction Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have achieved remarkable progress in recent years, enabling high-fidelity and semantically controllable image synthesis across diverse domains [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Inspired by the success of reinforcement learning for alignment in large language models, a growing number of post-training strategies have recently been introduced for diffusion models to improve human preference alignment, aesthetic quality, and prompt consistency [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Most existing approaches rely on training a reward model to learn preference signals and guide policy optimization. Diffusion-DPO [ 10 ] , which adapts Direct Preference Optimization [ 11 ] to diffusion models, has emerged as a practical alignment approach. It directly optimizes pairwise preferences through implicit likelihood comparisons while avoiding explicit reward model training, substantially simplifying the alignment pipeline. Following Diffusion-DPO, numerous variants have been proposed to improve aspects such as reward modeling, sampling efficiency, optimization stability, and model adaptability in diffusion alignment [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] . Despite these advances, we find that DPO-based alignment of diffusion models still suffers from a previously overlooked geometric failure mode: off-manifold drift. The manifold hypothesis posits that natural image distributions concentrate near a low-dimensional manifold embedded in the ambient latent denoising space [ 16 , 17 ] . In diffusion models, preference optimization is performed in the noisy latent denoising space conditioned on the text prompt, where the local geometry evolves across diffusion timesteps. However, although preference signals are ultimately defined over natural images, optimization is still performed in the full high-dimensional latent denoising space without considering the intrinsic geometry of the underlying data manifold. In particular, existing DPO-style objectives [ 10 ] optimize denoising prediction errors under an isotropic Euclidean metric, implicitly treating all perturbation directions in the latent space equally. This leads to two consequences: • Updates along manifold-normal directions can easily push samples away from the natural image manifold, causing semantic distortion and quality degradation. Without explicit suppression of these geometry-sensitive directions, off-manifold drift accumulates during alignment. • Updates along manifold-tangent directions are generally safer and often capture semantically meaningful variations. However, they are constrained by the same uniform regularization strength, unnecessarily limiting flexible semantic adjustments in preference optimization. While some prior works have incorporated manifold-aware geometric constraints into generative dynamics, such considerations remain largely unexplored in post-training preference alignment for pretrained diffusion models. To address this issue, we propose Anisotropic Geometry-Aware Preference Optimization (APO) . APO constructs a Jacobian-induced anisotropic metric from the local score-field geometry of the frozen reference model, adaptively suppressing updates along geometry-sensitive normal directions while allowing more flexible exploration along manifold-aligned tangent directions. To make the method computationally practical, we further derive an efficient forward-only approximation based on Hutchinson estimation and finite differences, eliminating the expensive reference-model backward pass while preserving the geometric regularization effect. Our key observations and technical contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify off-manifold drift as a fundamental geometric failure mode in DPO-based diffusion alignment, and provide theoretical and empirical analyses connecting this phenomenon to isotropic optimization in high-dimensional denoising space. • We propose APO, a Jacobian-induced anisotropic preference optimization framework together with an efficient forward-only Hutchinson finite-difference approximation, enabling scalable geometry-aware diffusion alignment without reference-model backpropagation. • Extensive experiments on SD1.5 and SDXL across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that APO consistently improves alignment quality, image realism, semantic preservation, and generation diversity while maintaining strong training efficiency. 2 Related Works Diffusion Models for Visual Generation Diffusion models have emerged as the dominant paradigm for image synthesis due to their training stability and high sample quality [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] . The introduction of latent diffusion substantially reduced computational costs by operating the denoising process in a compressed representation space, enabling high-resolution text-to-image generation at scale [ 1 ] . This architecture catalyzed a series of large-scale open-weight models, including SDXL [ 2 ] , SD3 [ 3 ] , and the FLUX series [ 4 ] , which form the backbone of most contemporary visual generation research. However, diffusion models are often trained on large-scale general-purpose datasets with varying quality, which tends to introduce biases that deviate from human preferences. Therefore, aligning diffusion models with human preferences is a highly necessary practice. Reward-Based Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Early post-training efforts adopt supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on curated high-quality image-text pairs [ 22 ] . While effective, SFT inherently treats all samples equally and does not capture the comparative nature of human preference. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) [ 23 , 24 ] addresses this by first training a proxy reward model on human annotations and then optimizing the diffusion policy with policy gradient methods such as DDPO [ 5 ] and DPOK [ 6 ] , or by directly backpropagating differentiable rewards as in DRaFT [ 8 ] and AlignProp [ 7 ] . These approaches, however, are prone to reward overoptimization. To bypass explicit reward learning, Diffusion-DPO [ 10 ] adapts Direct Preference Optimization to diffusion models, enabling offline fine-tuning directly on pairwise preference data without a separate reward model. Subsequently, a series of methods have been proposed to address the weaknesses of Diffusion-DPO in various aspects, including sampling efficiency, reward estimation, model adaptability, and reward diversity [ 25 , 12 , 26 , 13 , 27 , 15 , 28 , 29 ] . In addition, online reinforcement learning methods such as Flow-GRPO [ 9 ] and DanceGRPO [ 30 ] have become an increasingly popular paradigm. Some of these approaches seek to unify tasks spanning text-to-image, text-to-video, and image-to-video generation within a single framework, while others focus on improving computational efficiency [ 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 ] . While existing alignment methods primarily modify the reward formulation, optimization strategy, or sampling efficiency, our work instead revisits the geometric assumptions underlying the optimization metric itself. Manifold Learning for Diffusion The manifold hypothesis posits that high-dimensional natural data concentrate near a low-dimensional submanifold of the ambient space [ 16 , 17 ] . In the context of diffusion models, this connection is theoretically well-grounded: the score function is intimately related to the geometry of the data distribution and approximates the normal bundle of the data manifold [ 20 , 36 , 37 , 38 ] , a structural prior that has motivated a rich line of research connecting manifold learning with generative modeling [ 39 , 40 , 41 , 38 , 42 ] . Furthermore, manifold awareness has proven essential for improving inference-time quality, as demonstrated by CFG++ [ 43 ] , TCFG [ 44 ] , and Be Tangential to Manifold [ 45 ] . However, in the domain of preference alignment for diffusion models based on standard Euclidean diffusion parameterizations, manifold learning theory has yet to be considered. 3 Background and Motivation In this section, we first review diffusion models and the formulation of Diffusion-DPO. Under the manifold hypothesis [ 16 , 17 ] , however, natural data concentrate near a low-dimensional latent submanifold ℳ ⊂ ℝ D \mathcal{M}\subset\mathbb{R}^{D} , and the ambient space locally decomposes into tangent directions T x ​ ℳ T_{x}\mathcal{M} and normal directions N x ​ ℳ N_{x}\mathcal{M} . These directions play fundamentally different geometric roles. Reverse-trajectory displacements along tangent directions tend to preserve semantic consistency and remain close to the data manifold, whereas displacements along normal directions are more likely to move trajectories away from the manifold and degrade image quality. DPO-style diffusion alignment methods measure all trajectory-update discrepancies isotropically under the same Euclidean geometry, without distinguishing geometry-preserving directions from geometry-sensitive ones. As a result, updates along geometry-sensitive manifold-normal directions are insufficiently constrained, while manifold-aligned tangent directions become unnecessarily restricted for semantic adjustment. We refer to this geometric failure mode as off-manifold drift . This observation motivates the central question of our work: can we design a geometry-aware anisotropic regularizer that adapts to the local structure of the diffusion representation space?
